question: In 2023, there were 500 000 inmates in the EU’s prisons. Most prisons do not offer any professional activities, even though work is a major factor in rehabilitation. When jobs are offered, they are mostly linked to the running of the prison. Some prison boards, however, make prisoners available to private companies.

These underpaid jobs allow the companies concerned to boost their profits at the expense of any genuine rehabilitation schemes. This is particularly the case in Spain, where piecework – which has been banned in France since 2009 – is legal in prisons. French companies are exporting their production to Spain.

Veripack Embalajes, for example, is a Spanish subsidiary of the GUILLIN Group, a French packaging company that takes advantage of the infrastructure put in place by the prison authorities in Catalonia. In Europe, almost 300 companies are registered in Spanish prisons.

In addition to the social dumping that this produces, prison labour does not allow for inmates who work to be properly medically monitored, nor does it guarantee satisfactory conditions for labour inspectorates. In light of the above, does the Commission intend to: 1.
take action to ensure fundamental and individual freedoms are upheld in EU prisons?
bring in EU rules on work for prisoners, the main objective of which would be rehabilitation?
abolish piecework and guarantee a minimum wage throughout the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (19.12.2025) Detention issues are primarily within the responsibility of the Member States. To complement and support Member States’ policies, on 8 December 2022, the Commission presented the Recommendation on the procedural rights of suspects and accused in pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions1, a legally non-binding instrument.

One of the guiding principles of this Recommendation is that Member States are encouraged to manage detention in such a way as to facilitate the social rehabilitation of detainees. Paragraphs 47 and 48 of the Recommendation provide specific guidance on the work of detainees to promote their reintegration into society.

The Commission will publish a report in 2026 assessing the national measures taken by Member States to implement the Recommendation. It is primarily the responsibility of the Member States to ensure the correct application of the relevant legal provisions applicable to inmates, including where inmates may classify as workers.

As regards minimum wages, the Minimum Wage Directive2 applies to imprisoned persons as long as they have an employment relationship as defined by national law, with consideration to the case-law of the Court of Justice.

In these cases, Article 6 of the Directive requires Member States to ensure that variations of the statutory minimum wage for this specific group of workers, if they exist, respect the principles of non-discrimination and proportionality.
1 Commission Recommendation (EU) 2023/681 of 8 December 2022 on procedural rights of suspects and

accused persons subject to pre-trial detention and on material detention conditions, OJ L 86, 24.3.2023, pp. 44– 57. 2 Directive (EU) 2022/2041 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on adequate minimum wages in the European Union, OJ L 275, 25.10.2022, pp. 33–47.
